text: You want to check whether a list of `n` numbers contains any duplicate in O(n) average time. What should you keep track of as you scan?
options: A stack of the numbers seen so far
A queue of the numbers seen so far
A set of the numbers seen so far
answer: A set of the numbers seen so far

text: What is a hash collision?
options: The same key is inserted twice
The table runs out of free memory
A key is looked up before it is inserted
Two different keys map to the same bucket
answer: Two different keys map to the same bucket

text: Which of these can be used as a key in a Python dict?
What happens when you assign `d[k] = v` and the key `k` is already in the dict `d`?
options: A second entry for `k` is added
The old value is replaced and the size stays the same
It raises an error because `k` exists
The old value is kept and `v` is ignored
answer: The old value is replaced and the size stays the same

text: For two sets `a` and `b`, what does the intersection `a & b` contain?
options: Elements that are in both `a` and `b`
Elements in exactly one of `a` and `b`
answer: Elements that are in both `a` and `b`

text: In a hash table that uses separate chaining, where does a colliding key go?
options: Into the next empty bucket in the array
Into a bucket chosen at random
Into a list (chain) stored at the same bucket
answer: Into a list (chain) stored at the same bucket

text: In open addressing with linear probing, what happens when a key's home slot is already taken?
options: It tries the following slots one by one until it finds an empty one
It appends the key to a list stored in that slot
It doubles the table size immediately
It overwrites the key already in the slot
answer: It tries the following slots one by one until it finds an empty one

text: Why can't a Python list be used as a dict key?
options: Lists are too large to hash
It is mutable, so its hash could change after insertion and the entry would be lost
Lists keep their elements in order
answer: It is mutable, so its hash could change after insertion and the entry would be lost

text: Solving two-sum by storing each value's index in a hash map as you scan gives which complexity?
options: O(n^2) time and O(1) extra space
O(n log n) time and O(1) extra space
O(n) time and O(n) extra space
O(n) time and O(1) extra space
answer: O(n) time and O(n) extra space

text: In Python 3.7 and later, in what order does `for k in d` visit the keys of a dict?
options: The order the keys were first inserted
A random order that changes each run
Increasing order of the keys' hash values
answer: The order the keys were first inserted

text: In a linear-probing hash table, how should a key be deleted so later lookups still work?
options: Set the slot back to empty
Mark the slot as deleted (a tombstone) so probes continue past it
Move the last element of the array into the slot
Do nothing; deleted keys are found and skipped automatically
answer: Mark the slot as deleted (a tombstone) so probes continue past it

answer: Returns `d[k]` if `k` exists; otherwise stores `[]` under `k` and returns that list

text: A hash table doubles its bucket array (rehashing every key) whenever it gets too full. What is the amortized cost of an insert?
options: O(n), because any insert may trigger a resize
O(1), because the O(n) resizes happen geometrically rarely
O(log n), one for each doubling so far
O(1) in the worst case for every single insert
answer: O(1), because the O(n) resizes happen geometrically rarely

text: What is the worst-case lookup time in a separate-chaining hash table with `n` keys, and when does it happen?
options: O(1), because hashing always takes constant time
O(log n), when the table is completely full
O(n), when every key lands in the same bucket
O(n^2), while the table is being resized
answer: O(n), when every key lands in the same bucket

text: In the prefix-sum solution for "count subarrays whose sum is `k`", why is the map initialised to `{0: 1}`?
options: So subarrays that start at index 0 (prefix sum exactly `k`) are counted
So negative numbers in the array are handled
So the same subarray is never counted twice
So the map is never empty when `k` is 0
answer: So subarrays that start at index 0 (prefix sum exactly `k`) are counted

text: Why does "count subarrays with sum `k`" need a prefix-sum hash map instead of a two-pointer sliding window?
options: A sliding window only works on sorted arrays
The array may contain negative numbers, so growing the window does not always increase the sum
A sliding window needs O(n) extra space
answer: The array may contain negative numbers, so growing the window does not always increase the sum

text: Longest consecutive sequence: put all numbers in a set, then for each `x` with `x - 1` not in the set, walk `x + 1, x + 2, ...`. Why is this O(n) overall?
options: Sets keep their elements sorted, so runs sit next to each other
Removing duplicates makes the input no longer than the answer
Each number is walked over only once, from the start of its run
Each set lookup is O(log n), and there are only n / log n of them
answer: Each number is walked over only once, from the start of its run

text: Which pair of structures lets an LRU cache do both `get` and `put` in O(1) time?
options: A hash map plus a min-heap keyed by last access time
A sorted array of keys ordered by last access time
Two hash maps: key to value, and value to key
A hash map from key to node, plus a doubly linked list ordered by recency
answer: A hash map from key to node, plus a doubly linked list ordered by recency
